title: Using Categorical Covariates with AddiVortes
text: categorical variable d distinct levels treated number natural ordering magnitude categories. example, assigning “North” = 1, “South” = 2, “East” = 3, “West” = 4 incorrectly imply “West” four times “North”. One-hot encoding converts categorical variable d levels d − 1 binary (0/1) indicator columns. One level chosen reference level (convention, first level alphabetical order), remaining d − 1 levels receive column: reference level (“East” , alphabetically first) represented zeros. Using d − 1 rather d columns avoids perfect collinearity retaining full information group membership.

title: Using Categorical Covariates with AddiVortes
text: one-hot encoding, indicator column takes values 0 1, continuous covariates normalised range [−0.5, 0.5]. catScaling = 1 (default), binary jump 0 1 magnitude comparable full range normalised continuous covariate, giving categorical continuous covariates roughly equal influence Voronoi tessellation distances. can adjust catScaling argument: catScaling > 1: gives categorical differences weight continuous differences. catScaling < 1: gives categorical differences less weight, making model rely heavily continuous covariates. column name binary indicator follows pattern <original_column>_<level>. example, column region levels "East", "North", "South", "West" produces columns region_North, region_South, region_West ("East" reference). catScaling applies cat.onehot = TRUE. title: Using Categorical Covariates with AddiVortes

title: Using Categorical Covariates with AddiVortes
text: create dataset 400 observations two continuous covariates two categorical covariates. response variable depends four: Note region 4 levels product 3 levels. one-hot encoding become 3 2 binary columns respectively — total 5 extra columns alongside 2 continuous covariates. Eskin distance remain 2 categorical columns.
code: library(AddiVortes)  set.seed(123) n <- 400  x <- data.frame(   age = rnorm(n, mean = 40, sd = 10),   income = runif(n, 20, 120), # income in thousands   region = sample(c("East", "North", "South", "West"), n, replace = TRUE),   product = sample(c("Basic", "Premium", "Deluxe"), n, replace = TRUE),   stringsAsFactors = FALSE )  # True response: depends on continuous and categorical variables region_effect <- ifelse(x$region == "North", 5,   ifelse(x$region == "South", -5, 0) ) product_effect <- ifelse(x$product == "Premium", 10,   ifelse(x$product == "Deluxe", 20, 0) )  y <- 0.3 * x$age +   0.1 * x$income +   region_effect +   product_effect +   rnorm(n, sd = 3)

title: Using Categorical Covariates with AddiVortes
text: Fitting model identical standard workflow — simply pass data frame character factor columns directly. AddiVortes handles encoding internally (cat.onehot = TRUE default). encoding metadata stored fit$catEncoding automatically used making predictions, new data passed predict() encoded exactly reference levels.
code:
# Split into training and test sets set.seed(42) train_idx <- sample(n, 300)  x_train <- x[train_idx, ] y_train <- y[train_idx] x_test <- x[-train_idx, ] y_test <- y[-train_idx]  fit <- AddiVortes(   y = y_train,   x = x_train,   m = 50,   totalMCMCIter = 500,   mcmcBurnIn = 100,   catScaling = 1, # default: binary columns span [0, 1]   cat.onehot = TRUE, # default: one-hot encoding   showProgress = FALSE ) cat("In-sample RMSE:", round(fit$inSampleRmse, 3), "
") #> In-sample RMSE: 2.206  # The catEncoding field records how the encoding was built cat("
Reference levels used:
") #>  #> Reference levels used: for (j in fit$catEncoding$catColIndices) {   orig_col <- fit$catEncoding$origColNames[j]   ref_lev <- fit$catEncoding$colEncodings[[j]]$levels[1]   all_lev <- fit$catEncoding$colEncodings[[j]]$levels   cat(     " ", orig_col, ": reference =", ref_lev,     "| all levels:", paste(all_lev, collapse = ", "), "

title: Using Categorical Covariates with AddiVortes
text: Predictions new data work usual way. new data contains categorical levels training data, encoding applied consistently.
code: preds <- predict(fit, x_test, showProgress = FALSE) rmse_test <- sqrt(mean((y_test - preds)^2)) cat("Test RMSE:", round(rmse_test, 3), "\n") #> Test RMSE: 3.085 # Colour observations by product category prod_cols <- c("Basic" = "steelblue", "Premium" = "darkorange", "Deluxe" = "darkgreen") point_cols <- prod_cols[x_test$product]  plot(y_test, preds,   col = point_cols, pch = 19, cex = 0.8,   xlab = "Observed values",   ylab = "Predicted values",   main = "Predicted vs. Observed (coloured by product category)" ) abline(0, 1, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "grey40") legend("topleft",   legend = names(prod_cols),   col = prod_cols,   pch = 19, title = "Product", bty = "n" )

title: Using Categorical Covariates with AddiVortes
text: prediction time one-hot encoding, new observation contains category level seen training, AddiVortes treats reference level (binary indicators set zero). sensible default: model infer anything previously unseen level falls back baseline.
code: # Create a test point with an unseen product level "Luxury" x_new <- data.frame(   age = 45,   income = 80,   region = "North",   product = "Luxury", # unseen level   stringsAsFactors = FALSE ) pred_new <- predict(fit, x_new, showProgress = FALSE) cat(   "Prediction for unseen category 'Luxury' (treated as 'Basic'):",   round(pred_new, 3), "\n" ) #> Prediction for unseen category 'Luxury' (treated as 'Basic'): 25.954

title: Using Categorical Covariates with AddiVortes
text: catScaling parameter controls much influence categorical differences distance calculations one-hot encoding. fit two models — one catScaling = 1 (equal weight) one catScaling = 2 (double weight categorical differences) — compare test RMSEs. example, true response substantial category effects (±20 units product type) relative continuous effects, increasing catScaling may help model focus categorical group membership.

title: Classification with AddiVortes
text: AddiVortes() looks y: factor, character logical vector classification. Two levels give binary model; three give multinomial model. numeric vector exactly two unique values {0, 1} binary classification (1 event class). numeric vector Gaussian regression, previous versions package. first factor level reference class, matching glm(). numeric 0/1 data, 0 reference. Character vectors converted factor(), levels alphabetical. Missing values y allowed, classification response must least two classes.

title: Classification with AddiVortes
text: simulate two-dimensional problem whose labels follow simple linear boundary. predict(..., type = "response") returns posterior mean Φ(G(x))\Phi(G(x)), probability event class (active ). type = "class" returns labels, type = "quantile" gives credible intervals probabilities. Observations probability near 0.5 uncertain. 90% intervals typically cover 0.5 points.
code: set.seed(2026) n <- 120 x <- data.frame(   x1 = runif(n, -1, 1),   x2 = runif(n, -1, 1) ) y <- factor(ifelse(x$x1 + x$x2 > 0, "active", "inactive"),             levels = c("inactive", "active"))  fit_bin <- AddiVortes(   y, x,   m = 200,   totalMCMCIter = 2000,   mcmcBurnIn = 500,   showProgress = FALSE )  fit_bin$task #> [1] "binary" fit_bin$classLevels #> [1] "inactive" "active" fit_bin$inSampleAccuracy #> [1] 0.9916667 p_hat <- predict(fit_bin, x, type = "response", showProgress = FALSE) y_hat <- predict(fit_bin, x, type = "class", showProgress = FALSE) p_int <- predict(fit_bin, x,   type = "quantile",   quantiles = c(0.05, 0.95),   showProgress = FALSE )  mean(y_hat == y) #> [1] 0.9916667 range(p_hat) #> [1] 0.01799616 0.96853534 head(cbind(prob = round(p_hat, 3), lower = round(p_int[, 1], 3),            upper = round(p_int[, 2], 3), class = as.character(y_hat))) #>      prob    lower   upper   class      #> [1,] "0.724" "0.467" "0.921" "active"   #> [2,] "0.048" "0.004" "0.141" "inactive" #> [3,] "0.091" "0.011" "0.243" "inactive" #> [4,] "0.713" "0.438" "0.92"  "active"   #> [5,] "0.3"   "0.088" "0.565" "inactive" #> [6,] "0.033" "0"     "0.13"  "inactive" plot(p_hat, as.integer(y) - 1,      xlab = "Predicted P(active)",      ylab = "Observed class",      pch = 19, col = "steelblue") abline(v = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "grey40")

title: Classification with AddiVortes
text: three classes, AddiVortes fits K−1K-1 latent ensembles. argument m number tessellations per latent, three-class model m = 15 uses 30 tessellations total. type = "response" now n×Kn \times K matrix class probabilities. Rows sum 1. type = "class" returns class largest probability.
code: set.seed(2026) n3 <- 90 x3 <- data.frame(   x1 = rnorm(n3),   x2 = rnorm(n3) ) y3 <- cut(x3$x1, breaks = c(-Inf, -0.5, 0.5, Inf), labels = c("low", "mid", "high"))  fit_multi <- AddiVortes(   y3, x3,   m = 200,   totalMCMCIter = 2000,   mcmcBurnIn = 500,   showProgress = FALSE )  fit_multi$task #> [1] "multinomial" fit_multi$nLatents #> [1] 2 fit_multi$inSampleAccuracy #> [1] 0.9888889 p3 <- predict(fit_multi, x3, type = "response", showProgress = FALSE) cls3 <- predict(fit_multi, x3, type = "class", showProgress = FALSE)  head(round(p3, 3)) #>        low   mid  high #> [1,] 0.129 0.400 0.472 #> [2,] 0.682 0.230 0.088 #> [3,] 0.126 0.685 0.189 #> [4,] 0.195 0.671 0.135 #> [5,] 0.453 0.389 0.158 #> [6,] 0.843 0.107 0.050 mean(abs(rowSums(p3) - 1) < 1e-8) #> [1] 1 table(predicted = cls3, observed = y3) #>          observed #> predicted low mid high #>      low   30   0    0 #>      mid    0  34    1 #>      high   0   0   25

title: Machine Learning with AddiVortes: A Bayesian Alternative to BART
text: First, load AddiVortes package. example, use well-known Boston Housing dataset, included within package Boston.
code: # Load the package require(AddiVortes)  # Separate predictors (X) and the response variable (Y) X_Boston <- as.matrix(Boston[, 1:13]) Y_Boston <- as.numeric(as.matrix(Boston[, 14]))

title: Machine Learning with AddiVortes: A Bayesian Alternative to BART
text: evaluate model’s performance, need split data training set testing set. use standard 5/6 split training 1/6 testing.
code: n <- length(Y_Boston)  # Set a seed for reproducibility set.seed(1025)  # Create a training set containing 5/6 of the data TrainSet <- sort(sample.int(n, 5 * n / 6))  # The remaining data will be our test set TestSet <- setdiff(1:n, TrainSet)

title: Machine Learning with AddiVortes: A Bayesian Alternative to BART
text: Now can run main AddiVortes function training data. specify several parameters algorithm, number iterations trees.
code: # Run the AddiVortes algorithm on the training data results <- AddiVortes(   y = Y_Boston[TrainSet],   x = X_Boston[TrainSet, ],   m = 200,   totalMCMCIter = 2000,   mcmcBurnIn = 500,   nu = 6,   q = 0.85,   k = 3,   sd = 0.8,   Omega = 3,   LambdaRate = 25,   InitialSigma = "Linear",   showProgress = FALSE )

title: Machine Learning with AddiVortes: A Bayesian Alternative to BART
text: trained model object, can now make predictions unseen test data. calculate Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) see well model performed.
code: # Generate predictions on the test set preds <- predict(results,   X_Boston[TestSet, ],   showProgress = FALSE )  # The RMSE is contained in the results object cat("In-Sample RMSE:", results$inSampleRmse, "\n") #> In-Sample RMSE: 0.6772973  # Calculate the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) for the test set rmse <- sqrt(mean((Y_Boston[TestSet] - preds)^2)) cat("Test Set RMSE:", rmse, "\n") #> Test Set RMSE: 3.388859

title: Machine Learning with AddiVortes: A Bayesian Alternative to BART
text: Finally, good way assess model plot predicted values true values. perfect model, points lie equality line (y = x). also plot prediction intervals visualise model’s uncertainty.
code: # Plot true values vs. predicted values plot(Y_Boston[TestSet],   preds,   xlab = "True Values",   ylab = "Predicted Values",   main = "AddiVortes Predictions vs True Values",   xlim = range(c(Y_Boston[TestSet], preds)),   ylim = range(c(Y_Boston[TestSet], preds)),   pch = 19, col = "darkblue" )  # Add the line of equality (y = x) for reference abline(a = 0, b = 1, col = "darkred", lwd = 2)  # Get quantile predictions to create error bars/intervals preds_quantile <- predict(results,   X_Boston[TestSet, ],   "quantile",   showProgress = FALSE )  # Add error segments for each prediction for (i in seq_len(nrow(preds_quantile))) {   segments(Y_Boston[TestSet][i], preds_quantile[i, 1],     Y_Boston[TestSet][i], preds_quantile[i, 2],     col = "darkblue", lwd = 1   ) } legend("topleft",   legend = c("Prediction", "y=x Line", "95% Interval"),   col = c("darkblue", "darkred", "darkblue"),   lty = 1, pch = c(19, NA, NA), lwd = 2 )

title: Bayesian Regression and Prediction with AddiVortes
text: start creating 5-dimensional dataset. response variable Y determined simple rule based first two predictors, X[,1] X[,2], plus random noise. allows us know “true” data-generating process, useful evaluating model.
code: # Load the package library(AddiVortes)  # --- Generate Training Data --- set.seed(42) # for reproducibility  # Create a 5-column matrix of predictors X <- matrix(runif(2500), ncol = 5) X[, 1] <- -10 - X[, 1] * 10 X[, 2] <- X[, 2] * 100 X[, 3] <- -9 + X[, 3] * 10 X[, 4] <- 8 + X[, 4] X[, 5] <- X[, 5] * 10  # Create the response 'Y' based on a rule and add noise Y_underlying <- ifelse(-1 * X[, 2] > 10 * X[, 1] + 100, 10, 0) Y <- Y_underlying + rnorm(length(Y_underlying))  # Visualise the relationships in the data # The colours show the two underlying groups pairs(X,   col = ifelse(Y_underlying == 10, "red", "blue"),   pch = 19, cex = 0.5,   main = "Structure of Predictor Variables" )

title: Bayesian Regression and Prediction with AddiVortes
text: Next, fit AddiVortes model training data. example, ’ll use small number trees (m=50) quick demonstration. -sample RMSE gives us idea well model fits data trained . However, true test model performance new data.
code: # Fit the model AModel <- AddiVortes(Y, X, m = 50, showProgress = FALSE) # We can check the in-sample Root Mean Squared Error cat("In-sample RMSE:", AModel$inSampleRmse, "\n") #> In-sample RMSE: 0.8874636

title: Bayesian Regression and Prediction with AddiVortes
text: evaluate model’s predictive power, generate new “--sample” test set using process . use predict() method fitted model (AModel) get predictions new data. type = "response" returns predictions original response units. type = "link" returns latent model-scale function G(x)G(x) final unscaling step.
code: # --- Generate Test Data --- set.seed(101) # Use a different seed for the test set testX <- matrix(runif(1000), ncol = 5) testX[, 1] <- -10 - testX[, 1] * 10 testX[, 2] <- testX[, 2] * 100 testX[, 3] <- -9 + testX[, 3] * 10 testX[, 4] <- 8 + testX[, 4] testX[, 5] <- testX[, 5] * 10  # Create the true test response values testY_underlying <- ifelse(-1 * testX[, 2] > 10 * testX[, 1] + 100, 10, 0) testY <- testY_underlying + rnorm(length(testY_underlying))  # --- Make Predictions --- # Predict the mean response preds <- predict(AModel, testX,   showProgress = FALSE )  # Predict the latent sum of tessellations on the model scale preds_link <- predict(AModel, testX,   type = "link",   showProgress = FALSE )  # Predict the 90% credible interval (from 0.05 to 0.95 quantiles) # By default, this uses interval = "credible" which only accounts for # uncertainty in the mean function preds_q <- predict(AModel, testX,   "quantile", c(0.05, 0.95),   showProgress = FALSE )  # For prediction intervals that also include the model's error variance # (similar to lm's prediction intervals), use interval = "prediction" # preds_q_pred <- predict(AModel, testX, #                         "quantile", c(0.05, 0.95), #                         interval = "prediction", #                         showProgress = FALSE)

title: Bayesian Regression and Prediction with AddiVortes
text: plot effective way visualise model’s performance. plot observed values test set model’s predicted mean values. red lines plot represent true, underlying mean values (0 10) data-generating process. good model produce predictions cluster around lines. blue vertical segments represent 90% credible intervals prediction, giving us sense model’s uncertainty.  plot shows model successfully learned underlying structure data predictions clustering correctly around true mean values 0 10.
code: # Plot observed vs. predicted values plot(testY,   preds,   xlab = "Observed Values",   ylab = "Predicted Mean Values",   main = "Out-of-Sample Prediction Performance",   xlim = range(c(testY, preds_q)),   ylim = range(c(testY, preds_q)),   pch = 19, col = "darkblue" )  # Add error lines for the 90% credible interval for (i in seq_len(nrow(preds_q))) {   segments(testY[i], preds_q[i, 1],     testY[i], preds_q[i, 2],     col = rgb(0, 0, 0.5, 0.5), lwd = 1.5   ) }  # Add lines showing the true underlying means lines(c(min(testY) - 0.2, 3), c(0, 0), col = "pink", lwd = 3, lty = 2) lines(c(7, max(testY) + 0.2), c(10, 10), col = "pink", lwd = 3, lty = 2)  # Add a legend legend("bottomright",   legend = c(     "Predicted Mean & 90% Interval",     "True Underlying Mean"   ),   col = c("darkblue", "pink"),   pch = c(19, NA),   lty = c(1, 2),   lwd = c(1.5, 3),   bty = "n" )

title: Bayesian Regression and Prediction with AddiVortes
text: predict() method supports two types intervals, similar R’s built-lm function: Credible intervals (interval = "credible", default): reflect uncertainty mean function E[Y|X]. account posterior sampling variability uncertainty tessellation structure, include inherent noise individual observations. Prediction intervals (interval = "prediction"): include uncertainty mean function model’s error variance (σ²). makes appropriate predicting individual future observations. Let’s compare two types intervals subset test data:  can see plot, prediction intervals (red) wider credible intervals (blue). prediction intervals account : Epistemic uncertainty: uncertainty true mean function (captured credible interval) Aleatoric uncertainty: inherent random noise individual observations (additional width prediction intervals) can quantify difference: use type: Use credible intervals want understand uncertainty mean response given set predictor values (e.g., “average outcome type case?”) Use prediction intervals want predict individual future observations (e.g., “range outcomes expect specific new case?”) distinction standard regression lm, AddiVortes additionally captures complex non-linear relationships tessellation-based approach.
code:
# Use a subset of test data for clearer visualization subset_indices <- 1:20 testX_subset <- testX[subset_indices, ] testY_subset <- testY[subset_indices]  # Get credible intervals (uncertainty in mean only) cred_intervals <- predict(AModel, testX_subset,   type = "quantile",   interval = "credible",   quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975),   showProgress = FALSE )  # Get prediction intervals (includes error variance) pred_intervals <- predict(AModel, testX_subset,   type = "quantile",   interval = "prediction",   quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975),   showProgress = FALSE )  # Get mean predictions mean_preds <- predict(AModel, testX_subset,   type = "response",   showProgress = FALSE )  # Create comparison plot plot(seq_along(testY_subset), testY_subset,   xlab = "Observation Index",   ylab = "Response Value",   main = "Credible Intervals vs. Prediction Intervals",   pch = 19, col = "black", cex = 1.2, ylim = c(-5, 20) )  # Add mean predictions points(seq_along(testY_subset), mean_preds, pch = 4, col = "blue", cex = 1)  # Add credible intervals (narrower, in blue) for (i in seq_along(testY_subset)) {   segments(i, cred_intervals[i, 1],     i, cred_intervals[i, 2],     col = "blue", lwd = 2   ) }  # Add prediction intervals (wider, in red) for (i in seq_along(testY_subset)) {   segments(i - 0.1, pred_intervals[i, 1],     i - 0.1, pred_intervals[i, 2],     col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 1   ) }  # Add legend legend("topright",   legend = c(     "Observed Values", "Mean Prediction",     "95% Credible Interval", "95% Prediction Interval"   ),   col = c("black", "blue", "blue", "red"),   pch = c(19, 4, NA, NA),   lty = c(NA, NA, 1, 1),   lwd = c(NA, NA, 2, 2),   bty = "n" ) # Calculate average interval widths cred_width <- mean(cred_intervals[, 2] - cred_intervals[, 1]) pred_width <- mean(pred_intervals[, 2] - pred_intervals[, 1])  cat("Average 95% credible interval width:", round(cred_width, 2), "
") #> Average 95% credible interval width: 3.07 cat("Average 95% prediction interval width:", round(pred_width, 2), "
") #> Average 95% prediction interval width: 5.31 cat("Ratio (prediction/credible):", round(pred_width / cred_width, 2), "
") #> Ratio (prediction/credible): 1.73

title: Modelling Spherical Data with AddiVortes
text: Spherical data observations whose locations lie surface sphere. familiar example geographic data specified latitude longitude. Two important properties make different ordinary planar data: Wrap-around: Longitude values near −180° +180° actually close globe, Euclidean distance large. good distance metric must recognise . Curvature: Distances follow great-circle arcs (shortest path along sphere’s surface) rather straight lines. AddiVortes uses great-circle distance (also known geodesic distance haversine-type formula) metric = "S" specified. ensures points near poles near date line treated neighbours genuinely close sphere.

title: Modelling Spherical Data with AddiVortes
text: AddiVortes expects spherical coordinates radians, following convention: Latitude-type dimensions (spherical dimensions except last): values [−π/2, π/2]. Longitude / azimuthal dimension (last spherical column): values [−π, π]. single-surface model (globe), need exactly two columns: metric = "S". model use spherical (great-circle) distance pairs tessellation centres observations. data combine spherical non-spherical covariates, can pass vector metric indicators, e.g. metric = c(1, 1, 0) two spherical dimensions followed one Euclidean dimension.
code: x <- cbind(latitude_rad, longitude_rad)

title: Modelling Spherical Data with AddiVortes
text: simulate dataset 300 observations distributed across surface globe. observation latitude longitude, response variable represents smoothly varying quantity — , synthetic “temperature” warmest equator varies longitude. plot shows spatial distribution simulated response values:
code: library(AddiVortes)  set.seed(42) n <- 300  # Sample random locations on the globe lat <- runif(n, -pi / 2, pi / 2) # latitude in radians: [-pi/2, pi/2] lon <- runif(n, -pi, pi) # longitude in radians: [-pi, pi]  # True function: warmer at the equator, slight east-west gradient y_true <- 20 * cos(lat) + 5 * sin(lon)  # Add observation noise y <- y_true + rnorm(n, sd = 2)  # Covariate matrix: latitude first, longitude last (required convention) x <- cbind(lat, lon) # Colour scale for the response cols <- colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))(100) col_index <- cut(y, breaks = 100, labels = FALSE)  # Convert radians to degrees for a readable plot lat_deg <- lat * 180 / pi lon_deg <- lon * 180 / pi  plot(lon_deg, lat_deg,   col = cols[col_index], pch = 19, cex = 0.7,   xlab = "Longitude (degrees)",   ylab = "Latitude (degrees)",   main = "Simulated Response on the Globe" ) legend("bottomleft",   legend = c("High", "Low"),   col = c("red", "blue"),   pch = 19, bty = "n" )

title: Modelling Spherical Data with AddiVortes
text: fit AddiVortes metric = "S" tell model columns spherical coordinates. model use great-circle distance assigning observations Voronoi cells. comparison, fit identical model using default Euclidean metric. model treats latitude longitude ordinary continuous variables handle wrap-around near ±π correctly.
code: fit_sph <- AddiVortes(   y = y,   x = x,   m = 50,   totalMCMCIter = 500,   mcmcBurnIn = 100,   metric = "S", # use great-circle distance for all columns   showProgress = FALSE ) cat("In-sample RMSE (spherical metric):", round(fit_sph$inSampleRmse, 3), "\n") #> In-sample RMSE (spherical metric): 1.198 fit_euc <- AddiVortes(   y = y,   x = x,   m = 50,   totalMCMCIter = 500,   mcmcBurnIn = 100,   metric = "E", # Euclidean distance (default)   showProgress = FALSE ) cat("In-sample RMSE (Euclidean metric):", round(fit_euc$inSampleRmse, 3), "\n") #> In-sample RMSE (Euclidean metric): 1.386

title: Modelling Spherical Data with AddiVortes
text: generate held-test set compare two models. also include group observations near date line (longitude ≈ ±π) highlight Euclidean metric likely struggle.
code: set.seed(101) n_test <- 200  lat_test <- runif(n_test, -pi / 2, pi / 2) lon_test <- runif(n_test, -pi, pi)  y_true_test <- 20 * cos(lat_test) + 5 * sin(lon_test) y_test <- y_true_test + rnorm(n_test, sd = 2)  x_test <- cbind(lat_test, lon_test) preds_sph <- predict(fit_sph, x_test, showProgress = FALSE) preds_euc <- predict(fit_euc, x_test, showProgress = FALSE) rmse_sph <- sqrt(mean((y_test - preds_sph)^2)) rmse_euc <- sqrt(mean((y_test - preds_euc)^2))  cat("Test RMSE — spherical metric:", round(rmse_sph, 3), "\n") #> Test RMSE — spherical metric: 2.192 cat("Test RMSE — Euclidean metric:", round(rmse_euc, 3), "\n") #> Test RMSE — Euclidean metric: 2.095

title: Modelling Spherical Data with AddiVortes
text: plot shows predicted versus observed values models test set. well-calibrated model points lying close diagonal.
code: y_range <- range(c(y_test, preds_sph, preds_euc))  plot(y_test, preds_sph,   pch = 19, col = "darkblue", cex = 0.7,   xlab = "Observed values",   ylab = "Predicted values",   main = "Spherical vs. Euclidean Metric: Predicted vs. Observed",   xlim = y_range, ylim = y_range ) points(y_test, preds_euc, pch = 4, col = "darkred", cex = 0.7) abline(0, 1, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "grey40") legend("topleft",   legend = c("Spherical metric", "Euclidean metric", "y = x"),   col    = c("darkblue", "darkred", "grey40"),   pch    = c(19, 4, NA),   lty    = c(NA, NA, 2),   lwd    = c(NA, NA, 2),   bty    = "n" )

title: Modelling Spherical Data with AddiVortes
text: dataset contains covariates whose embedding separate n-spheres, must treated separately AddiVortes. augment data illustrate . try use AddiVortes , encounter error, since two azimuthal coordinates covariates. recitfy , provide AddiVortes additional argument, members, indicates coordinates belong space: case give first two coordinates membership 1, three membership 2. follow process ; fitting Euclidean coordinates, comparing results relative hold-test set.
code: lat_prime1 <- runif(n, -pi/2, pi/2) lat_prime2 <- runif(n, -pi/2, pi/2) lon_prime <- runif(n, -pi, pi)  y_prime_true <- 20 * cos(lat) + 5 * sin(lon) - 5 * cos(lat_prime1) * sin(lat_prime2) +   10*sin(lon_prime)^2 * sin(abs(lat_prime1 - lat_prime2)) y_prime <- y_prime_true + rnorm(n, sd = 3)  x_prime <- cbind(lat, lon, lat_prime1, lat_prime2, lon_prime) fit_sph_new <- AddiVortes(   y = y_prime,   x = x_prime,   m = 50,   totalMCMCIter = 500,   mcmcBurnIn = 100,   metric = "S", # use great-circle distance for all columns   showProgress = FALSE ) #> Error in `covariateStructure_internal()`: #> ! More than one spherical parameter in membership group 1 has range >pi. fit_sph_new <- AddiVortes(   y = y_prime,   x = x_prime,   m = 50,   totalMCMCIter = 500,   mcmcBurnIn = 100,   metric = "S", # use great-circle distance for all columns,   members = rep(1:2, times = c(2,3)), # indicate membership   showProgress = FALSE ) fit_euc_new <- AddiVortes(   y = y_prime,   x = x_prime,   m = 50,   totalMCMCIter = 500,   mcmcBurnIn = 100,   metric = "E", # Euclidean distance (default)   showProgress = FALSE ) ## Set up test data lat_prime_test1 <- runif(n_test, -pi/2, pi/2) lat_prime_test2 <- runif(n_test, -pi/2, pi/2) lon_prime_test <- runif(n_test, -pi, pi)  y_prime_test_true <- 20 * cos(lat_test) + 5 * sin(lon_test) - 5 * cos(lat_prime_test1) * sin(lat_prime_test2) +   10*sin(lon_prime_test)^2 * sin(abs(lat_prime_test1 - lat_prime_test2)) y_prime_test <- y_prime_test_true + rnorm(n_test, sd = 3)  x_prime_test <- cbind(lat_test, lon_test, lat_prime_test1, lat_prime_test2, lon_prime_test)  ## Make predictions preds_prime_sph <- predict(fit_sph_new, x_prime_test, showProgress = FALSE) preds_prime_euc <- predict(fit_euc_new, x_prime_test, showProgress = FALSE)  rmse_prime_sph <- sqrt(mean((y_prime_test - preds_prime_sph)^2)) rmse_prime_euc <- sqrt(mean((y_prime_test - preds_prime_euc)^2))  cat("Test RMSE — spherical metric:", round(rmse_prime_sph, 3), "\n") #> Test RMSE — spherical metric: 3.762 cat("Test RMSE — Euclidean metric:", round(rmse_prime_euc, 3), "\n") #> Test RMSE — Euclidean metric: 3.837  y_prime_range <- range(c(y_prime_test, preds_prime_sph, preds_prime_euc))  plot(y_prime_test, preds_prime_sph,   pch = 19, col = "darkblue", cex = 0.7,   xlab = "Observed values",   ylab = "Predicted values",   main = "Spherical vs. Euclidean Metric: Predicted vs. Observed",   xlim = y_prime_range, ylim = y_prime_range ) points(y_prime_test, preds_prime_euc, pch = 4, col = "darkred", cex = 0.7) abline(0, 1, lwd = 2, lty = 2, col = "grey40") legend("topleft",   legend = c("Spherical metric", "Euclidean metric", "y = x"),   col    = c("darkblue", "darkred", "grey40"),   pch    = c(19, 4, NA),   lty    = c(NA, NA, 2),   lwd    = c(NA, NA, 2),   bty    = "n" )

title: Modelling Spherical Data with AddiVortes
text: Set metric = "S" (metric = "Spherical") use great-circle distance covariate columns. datasets mix spherical non-spherical covariates, pass vector 0s 1s, e.g. metric = c(1, 1, 0) two spherical dimensions one Euclidean dimension. datasets covariates taken multiple different spherical coordinate systems, pass vector membership indicate belongs . example, five covariates first three S3 remaining two S2, members = rep(1:2, times = c(3,2)). text: y vector response values. Numeric y treated regression, except exactly two unique values {0, 1}, binary classification. Factor, character logical vectors treated classification: two levels give binary probit model three levels give multinomial probit model. first factor level (0 numeric 0/1 responses) reference class. Missing values allowed. x matrix data frame covariates. Character factor columns treated categorical variables automatically converted d-1 binary indicator variables via one-hot encoding (first level reference). m number tessellations. multinomial classification number tessellations per latent dimension (\(K-1\) latents \(K\) classes). totalMCMCIter number MCMC iterations. Default 2000. mcmcBurnIn number burn-iterations. Default 500. nu degrees freedom inverse-gamma prior residual variance. Ignored classification, latent residual variance fixed 1. q quantile used set inverse-gamma prior residual variance. Ignored classification. k Prior scale tessellation output values. regression, \(\sigma_\mu = 0.5/(k\sqrt{m})\) scaled response. classification, \(\sigma_\mu = 3/(k\sqrt{m})\) latent probit scale. sd standard deviation used centre proposals. Omega Omega/(number covariates) prior probability adding dimension. LambdaRate rate Poisson distribution number centres. InitialSigma method used calculate initial residual variance regression ("Linear" "Naive"). Ignored classification. thinning thinning rate. metric Either "E" (Euclidean, default), "S" (Spherical), "C" (Categorical). members needed, indicates membership covariates different subspaces (needed using multiple spheres covariate space). Default NULL. catScaling Numeric scalar controlling scale binary indicator variables created categorical covariates. binary indicator takes values 0 (reference level) catScaling (non-reference level). default value 1 matches range continuous covariates, normalised [-0.5, 0.5] (range = 1) fitting, categorical differences receive comparable weight continuous differences distance calculations. Increase 1 give categorical differences weight; decrease 1 give less weight. Binary indicator columns named <colname>_<level> (e.g. column grp levels "", "B", "C" produces columns grp_B grp_C, "" reference level). cat.onehot categorical covariates one-hot encoded? Default TRUE. TRUE, categorical covariate d levels expanded d − 1 binary indicators distances Euclidean (weighted catScaling). FALSE, categories kept single integer-coded column mismatches use Eskin distance (Eskin et al., 2002), squared cost \(2 / d^2\) levels differ 0 match; catScaling ignored. See categorical covariates vignette comparison guidance use. showProgress Logical; TRUE, progress bar shown fitting.

code: # \donttest{ # Simple example with simulated data set.seed(123) x <- matrix(rnorm(50), 10, 5) y <- rnorm(10) # Fit model with reduced iterations for quick example fit <- AddiVortes(y, x, m = 5, totalMCMCIter = 50, mcmcBurnIn = 10)  # Larger example with categorical covariates (d=2 and d=3) and a test set set.seed(456) n_train <- 200 n_test <- 50 x_train <- data.frame(   x1   = rnorm(n_train),   x2   = runif(n_train),   grp2 = sample(c("A", "B"), n_train, replace = TRUE),   grp3 = sample(c("low", "mid", "high"), n_train, replace = TRUE) ) y_train <- x_train$x1 + ifelse(x_train$grp2 == "B", 1, 0) + rnorm(n_train, sd = 0.5)  fit2 <- AddiVortes(y_train, x_train,   m = 10, totalMCMCIter = 200, mcmcBurnIn = 50,   catScaling = 1, showProgress = FALSE )  x_test <- data.frame(   x1   = rnorm(n_test),   x2   = runif(n_test),   grp2 = sample(c("A", "B"), n_test, replace = TRUE),   grp3 = sample(c("low", "mid", "high"), n_test, replace = TRUE) ) y_test <- x_test$x1 + ifelse(x_test$grp2 == "B", 1, 0) + rnorm(n_test, sd = 0.5)  preds <- predict(fit2, x_test, showProgress = FALSE) test_rmse <- sqrt(mean((y_test - preds)^2))  # Binary classification is selected automatically from a 0/1 or factor y set.seed(789) x_clf <- matrix(runif(80), 40, 2) y_clf <- factor(ifelse(x_clf[, 1] + x_clf[, 2] > 1, "yes", "no")) fit_clf <- AddiVortes(y_clf, x_clf, m = 8, totalMCMCIter = 80,                       mcmcBurnIn = 20, showProgress = FALSE) p_clf <- predict(fit_clf, x_clf, type = "response", showProgress = FALSE) cls_clf <- predict(fit_clf, x_clf, type = "class", showProgress = FALSE) # }

title: Predict Method for AddiVortes — predict.AddiVortes
code: # \donttest{ # Fit a model set.seed(123) X <- matrix(rnorm(100), 20, 5) Y <- rnorm(20) fit <- AddiVortes(Y, X, m = 5, totalMCMCIter = 50, mcmcBurnIn = 10)  # New data for prediction X_new <- matrix(rnorm(25), 5, 5)  # Mean predictions pred_mean <- predict(fit, X_new, type = "response")  # Credible intervals (uncertainty in mean only) pred_conf <- predict(fit, X_new,   type = "quantile",   interval = "credible",   quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975) )  # Prediction intervals (includes error variance) pred_pred <- predict(fit, X_new,   type = "quantile",   interval = "prediction",   quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975) )  # Prediction intervals are wider than credible intervals mean(pred_pred[, 2] - pred_pred[, 1]) > mean(pred_conf[, 2] - pred_conf[, 1]) #> [1] TRUE # }
